1.pericope_label: Paul returns to Lystra and takes Timothy, well reported of by the brethren

schools.summary: Gill marks the courage of the return, that these were cities of Lycaonia and that in the second of them Paul had been stoned, yet he goes there again, none of these things moving him from the preaching of the gospel; on the report he says it is borne to Timothy himself and not to his father. Calvin says Luke states the good report plainly so that we may know Paul did nothing rashly or without good consideration, and that Paul here observes in his own case the choice he elsewhere commands in choosing ministers; he raises the apparent disagreement that Luke has the testimony come from the brethren while Paul requires a bishop to be well reported of by those without, and answers that we must principally look to the judgment of the godly, who alone are meet witnesses and alone discern rightly according to the Spirit of God, attributing no more to the wicked than to blind men, yet that in the second place even infidels should be brought to commend him, lest the Church be exposed to their slanders and evil speaking.

Henry treats the passage as an adoption, Paul a spiritual father taking a disciple of Christ to be his own disciple, and notes that one design of the book is to help us understand the epistles, two of which are addressed to this man; he names the mother Eunice and the grandmother Lois and commends both for their unfeigned faith. On the circumcision he says the entail of the covenant and its seal went, as other entails did in that nation, by the father and not by the mother, so that Timothy was neither obliged to circumcision nor entitled to it unless when grown he should himself desire it, and though his mother could not prevail to have him circumcised in infancy she educated him in the fear of God, that though he wanted the sign of the covenant he might not want the thing signified. On the marriage he holds the prohibition ran equally both ways, though it seems limited to the nations living among them in Canaan, from whom infection was most feared.

Clarke says Timothy must have been very young, since years afterwards there was still danger that his youth would prejudice his ministry, makes the father either a mere heathen or at most a proselyte of the gate who never submitted to circumcision, since had he submitted he would no doubt have circumcised his son, and notes that one editor would repunctuate the sentence so that the good report attaches plainly to Timothy and not to his father; he adds that Timothy had a very early religious education from his mother and grandmother, which prepared him for the work to which God now called him.

Barnes observes that Luke drops Barnabas at this point and confines the narrative to Paul, holds it impossible to determine which of the two towns Timothy belonged to, argues his youth from the later charge that no man despise it, infers from the son's uncircumcision that the father had not been circumcised either, and thinks the law against marriage with a woman of another nation was simply not much regarded by Jews living in the midst of heathen nations. Ellicott makes Timothy a native of Lystra, reads the verse as the first mention of a name afterwards so dear to the Apostle, sets his age at not more than eighteen or twenty, thinks the father probably a proselyte since the child had been trained in the sacred books from infancy and probably still living, and adds that a good report from Iconium as well as Lystra shows Timothy already employed in carrying on intercourse between the two churches. Robertson makes him a native of Lystra, puts him at about eighteen, argues that a proselyte father would have had him circumcised, finds in the imperfect a continuous witness borne in both towns, and draws the rule that the approval of the local church is a wise precaution before the licensing and ordaining of a preacher.

debates: Whether Timothy's father was a proselyte: Ellicott thinks it probable from the child's training in the sacred books, Clarke makes him a mere heathen or at most a proselyte of the gate, and Robertson and Barnes argue backwards from the son that a proselyte would have had him circumcised

Whose good report is required: Calvin harmonises Luke's testimony from the brethren with Paul's requirement that a bishop be well reported of by those without, ranking the judgment of the godly first and the enforced commendation of infidels second

Whether the intermarriage was lawful: Henry holds the prohibition ran equally both ways but seems limited to the nations living in Canaan, while Barnes thinks it was simply not much regarded by Jews living among the heathen
Where Timothy belonged: Barnes holds it impossible to determine between the two towns, while Robertson and Ellicott make him a native of Lystra
outliers: Ellicott's portrait of Timothy from the epistles: a constitution naturally not strong and later weakened by a rigorous asceticism, emotional even to tears, naturally shrinking from hardships and responsibilities yet facing them in the strength of Christ

Ellicott on the name, found in the Maccabean books of a general defeated by Judas Maccabeus and in early Christian inscriptions in the Vatican Museum, its meaning of one who honours God suiting the child of a proselyte
Robertson's aside that it is idle to ask whether Paul came on purpose to get Timothy to take Mark's place
Henry's point that though his mother could not have him circumcised she educated him in the fear of God, that though he wanted the sign of the covenant he might not want the thing signified
Clarke's report of an editor's repunctuation attaching the good report to Timothy rather than to his father

3.pericope_label: The circumcision of Timothy, the delivery of the decrees, and the strengthening of the churches

schools.summary: Gill notes the young man had not only the grace of God but considerable gifts for ministerial service, and a good testimony besides, so that Paul was very desirous of him as a companion, and adds that the churches were established both by the preaching of the gospel and by the decrees delivered. Calvin alone asks whether the sign could lawfully be used once its force was abolished: he holds the circumcision was no sacrament as Abraham's was but an indifferent ceremony serving only for the nourishing of love and not for any exercise of godliness, and sets out three degrees, that the ceremonies of the law were so abolished by the coming of Christ that they no longer belonged to the worship of God, were no longer figures of spiritual things, and carried no necessity; that their use nevertheless remained free until the truth of the gospel should more plainly appear; and that it was not lawful to retain them except so far as the use served for edification and fostered no superstition. He draws the line that decides the case, that circumcision did not stand where the sacrifices stood, which were ordained for the expiating of sins, so that it was lawful for Paul to circumcise Timothy and would not have been lawful for him to offer a sacrifice for sin. On the decrees he holds they continued only for a time, since as soon as Paul saw the danger of offence cease he unburdened the churches and made free what the apostles had forbidden, which cancels nothing they decreed because they never meant a perpetual law but only to mitigate for a short season what might hurt weak consciences; and treating the decrees as put in by the way, he says the far other fruit Luke commends is that the churches were confirmed in the faith, religion having the first place, whose sole foundation is faith staying itself on the pure Word of God and not depending on men's laws.

Clarke gives the plain practical reason for the circumcision, that the Jews would neither have heard Timothy preach nor had any connection with him otherwise, and that Paul himself could have had no access to them had they known he associated with an uncircumcised man, since they would have counted both unclean; the act was merely prudential, laid Timothy under no necessity of observing the ritual, and could not prejudice his spiritual state, because it was not done to seek justification by law, whereas in the case of Titus the object of those who pressed it was to bring him under the yoke of the law. On the decrees he reports an editor's contention that the term rendered decrees is a gloss and that only the things judged stood in the text originally, the Syriac reading instead the decrees that were written, and notes that our own term dogma is simply the Greek word in English letters; and he says the disputes at Antioch had spread far and unhinged many, so that the decrees came in good time to prevent further mischief. Wesley reduces the circumcision to the unbelieving Jews, to whom Paul designed Timothy should preach, and who would not have conversed with him at all so long as he was uncircumcised.

Barnes makes the choice exemplary: Paul looked up and called forth the talent that might be usefully employed in the church, since Timothy would plainly never have thought of it himself, and he sought and valued proper qualifications, a good reputation, talents and prudence, and a careful training in the Holy Scriptures; he reduces the circumcision to expediency for the sake of peace, in accordance with Paul's avowed principle of becoming to the Jews as a Jew, and takes the word rendered decrees for the proper term for the edict of a king or legislature, here carrying an obligation to submit, with an attested copy of the letter probably sent to the various Gentile churches. Robertson puts the difference from the case of Titus in the stakes, that there the whole principle of Gentile liberty was at issue whereas Timothy, being both Jew and Greek, would have given continual offence with no advantage to that cause and could not otherwise have preached in the synagogues at all, so that it was a question of efficient service and not an essential of salvation, and he cites another that Timothy was circumcised because of Jewish unbelievers and not because of Jewish believers; on the decrees he takes the perfect participle to emphasise the permanence of the conclusions reached at Jerusalem and the present infinitive to accent a charter of liberty for continual living and not a temporary compromise, finds in the imperfect a delivery kept up city after city and a proof of Paul's loyalty to the Jerusalem compact, and reads the verb of strengthening as making firm and solid like the muscles, with the increase a continuous revival. Ellicott gives three reasons for the circumcision, that the act was spontaneous and men may rightly concede as a favour what they would be justified in resisting when demanded as a necessity, that Titus was a Greek pure and simple while the mixed parentage of Timothy made him by the received canons inherit from the nobler side and stand by birth as an Israelite, and that by not urging circumcision before baptism or the breaking of bread the Apostle had already shown he did not hold it essential; on the decrees he argues that the sheer number of copies the process implies is itself a guarantee that Luke gives a faithful transcript.

debates: How the circumcision of Timothy squares with the refusal to circumcise Titus: Clarke makes the difference the object of those who pressed it, Robertson the stakes, Ellicott the spontaneity of the act and Timothy's descent from the nobler side, Barnes bare expediency for peace, and Calvin the standing of the rite itself
Whether the abolished ceremonies could lawfully be used at all: Calvin's three degrees, and his line that Paul might circumcise Timothy but might not have offered a sacrifice for sin

Whether the decrees were a permanent charter or a temporary mitigation: Robertson reads the participle and infinitive for permanence and a charter of liberty for continual living, expressly not a temporary compromise, while Calvin holds flatly that they continued only for a time and that Paul afterwards made free what the apostles had forbidden

What the word rendered decrees was: Clarke reports the contention that it is a gloss, with only the things judged standing originally and the Syriac reading the decrees that were written, while Barnes and Robertson take it for the proper term for a public edict
outliers: Barnes makes this an instance of calling forth latent talent in the church, and compares it to what education societies now attempt

Ellicott's remark that the acceptance of the seal by one grown to manhood without it shows the disciple had imbibed the spirit of his Master, and his suggestion that Timothy now took the place Mark had filled, chiefly as an attendant
Robertson's note that Silas's presence gave added dignity to the passing out of the decrees, since he had been one of the committee sent from Jerusalem
Robertson reads the imperfect of the father's being a Greek as possibly indicating that he was no longer living, against Ellicott's judgment on the preceding verses that he probably was
Calvin's use of the passage against those who charge the Reformed with being unlike Paul for governing consciences by the Word of God alone
Calvin's image of faith creeping abroad to others by branches, as those first called profit and so bring others to Christ

6.pericope_label: Forbidden to speak in Asia and Bithynia, and led down to Troas

schools.summary: Gill fills in the antiquities, deriving the name of Phrygia either from the river Phryx or from a word meaning dry, since it was a dry and sandy country famous for its marble, tracing the Phrygians through Josephus to Togarmah the son of Gomer, and reporting from Herodotus that they were called Briges while they were Europeans dwelling with the Macedonians and changed their name with their country on going into Asia; he adds the boundaries of the two Mysias and notes that they passed by Mysia without stopping. Calvin refuses every account of the prohibition that grounds the difference in the men: if it be answered that these Gentiles were unworthy of the doctrine of salvation, we may demand why Macedonia was worthier, and those who desire to be too wise assign the cause to men, that God vouchsafes his gospel as he sees a man bent to the obedience of faith, whereas he himself says far otherwise, that he appeared plainly to those who sought him not and spake to those who asked not of him, for whence comes aptness to be taught, or a mind to obey, but from his Spirit? He raises the pastoral question what certainty ministers can have today who are certified by no oracles when to speak or hold their peace, and answers that Paul's charge was so wide that he needed singular direction, having been sent to preach through Asia and Europe, which was to sail in a most wide sea, so that it is no wonder God beckoned to him in that confused wideness as by reaching forth his hand; and he observes that Paul was not a little encouraged to proceed when he knew the Spirit of God was his guide and the governor of his actions.

Henry offers three answers to the prohibition and prefers the third: that Asia did not need them, other hands being at work; that the people were not yet prepared, as they were afterwards; or, on a suggestion he takes from another, that Christ meant to employ Paul in a piece of new work, preaching to a Roman colony, since hitherto the Gentiles he had reached were Greeks and the Romans were more particularly hated by the Jews, whose armies were the abomination of desolation. He finds in it an intimation that the light of the gospel would in aftertimes be directed more westward than eastward. On how the prohibition came he suggests either secret whispers in the minds of both men, which they found on comparing notes to be the same and from the same Spirit, or prophets speaking from the Spirit, and observes that the removals of ministers and the dispensing of the means of grace by them are in a particular manner under divine guidance; he marks the difference from an older prohibition, that the prophet was forbidden to preach at all, where these are forbidden in one place only while directed to another of greater need. He also thinks the gospel had already been planted in Phrygia and Galatia, and probably by Paul himself.

Clarke makes the prohibition a matter of readiness, that God chose to send his servants where the word would be affectionately received, those in the western province not being sufficiently prepared as yet; he argues that the Asia named cannot be Asia Minor at large, since its provinces included the very districts where the apostles had just preached, so that only the proconsular province can be meant, containing Ionia, Aeolia and Lydia, where the seven churches were afterwards situated; he reports that many manuscripts and versions read the Spirit of Jesus rather than the Spirit, holds the reading undoubtedly genuine and would have it immediately restored to the text; and he traces the successive names of Troy from Dardanus, Tros and Ilus, notes that no ascertainable vestige of it remains so that some have even doubted its existence, and reports the site claimed for it twelve miles from the sea. Wesley takes the prohibition for an inward dictate and adds that a strong impression for which we are not able to give any account is not altogether to be despised, and says Paul had spoken in Phrygia and Galatia what was sufficient, the time for the proconsular province not being come.

Barnes says God intended to carry the gospel further into Greece and that this prohibition was the means of its first introduction into Europe, takes the forbidding for a direct revelation, identifies the Asia named with the proconsular province, also called Ionia, whose capital was Ephesus and in which the seven churches stood, and explains that Galatia was named by the Gauls who conquered and settled it, no less than three of their tribes having held it, with many Jews settled there besides, which is why so many parties could be formed and so much controversy arise between Jewish and Gentile converts. Robertson works the harder question, whether Luke's phrase names one region at once Phrygian and Galatian or adds a province to a district, sets out the northern and southern theories by name, and rests the case on grammar, that the aorist passive participle rendered having been forbidden can express only simultaneous or antecedent action and never subsequent, so that the topography brings Paul right up to Bithynia, which he calls the strongest argument for the northern view; he has them skirting Mysia and neglecting it without preaching, reaches Troas as the seaport counted part of neither province and the place to take ship for Philippi, and notes that the expression the Spirit of Jesus occurs nowhere else. Ellicott fills out Luke's outline from the epistle, that Paul was detained in Galatia by severe illness, in which many have seen the thorn in the flesh, and was received by the Galatians as an angel of God; he catches the tone of the whole stretch, the uncertainty produced day by day by this conflict between human plans and divine direction, agrees on the reading the Spirit of Jesus and finds it of some dogmatic importance as confirming that the Spirit stands in the same relation to the Son as to the Father, and ends where the vision begins, that the question which must have occupied all Paul's thoughts, where he was next to proclaim the glad tidings, expressed itself in prayer, and the vision was its answer.

debates: Why the Spirit forbade Asia and Bithynia: Henry prefers the design of a new work among Romans, Barnes the extension of the gospel into Greece, Clarke the unreadiness of the hearers, and Calvin refuses all three so far as they ground the difference in men, since God appeared plainly to those who sought him not
How the prohibition was conveyed: Henry by secret whispers in both minds, found identical when they compared notes, or by prophets; Barnes by direct revelation; Wesley by an inward dictate
What the Asia named here is: Clarke argues it cannot be Asia Minor at large, since the apostles had just preached in its provinces, and Barnes agrees in identifying it with the proconsular province

Where the Galatia of this verse lies: Robertson sets out the northern and southern theories and rests the case on the aorist participle, which cannot express subsequent action, so that the topography brings Paul up to Bithynia and yields the strongest argument for the northern view

Whether the text reads the Spirit or the Spirit of Jesus: Clarke calls the longer reading undoubtedly genuine and would restore it at once, Ellicott agrees and presses its dogmatic weight, and Robertson notes only that the phrase occurs nowhere else
outliers: Ellicott's account of the Galatians, who spoke a Keltic dialect like that spoken on the Moselle in the fourth century after Christ and kept the quickness of emotion and liability to sudden change of that temperament, and who had adopted the wild orgiastic worship of the Phrygian Earth-goddess with its eunuch-priests
Ellicott's reconstruction that Paul was detained by attacks of acute pain in the nerves of the eye, in which many writers have seen the thorn in the flesh
Ellicott's judgment that the poem which tells the tale of Ilium was probably unknown to Paul, and would have had no charms for him had it been otherwise
Robertson's protest against smashing Luke's grammar to pieces to bolster up a theory of criticism
Henry's contrast between the older prophet forbidden to preach at all and these ministers forbidden in one place only while directed to another of greater need
Calvin's image of a charge so wide that it was to sail in a most wide sea, God beckoning as by reaching forth his hand

9.pericope_label: The vision of the man of Macedonia, the crossing to Europe, and the arrival at Philippi

schools.summary: Gill takes the vision either as a dream or as seen waking, describes the strait that divided Asia from Europe, and fills in the history of Philippi, which was called Datos and then Crenidae from its many wholesome fountains before Philip rebuilt it and gave it his name, and which was famous for the battle in which Brutus and Cassius were vanquished. Calvin agrees with Wesley against a dream on the ground of the text, that it is not said the vision came in a dream but only in the night season, since there are night visions that men see waking, and adds that the Lord did not always observe the same manner of revelation, divers kinds being more convenient for confirmation; he turns to the word help, and says that since the gospel is the power of God to salvation its ministers are said to help those who perish, which should stir up godly teachers and teach the peoples to receive them as deliverers, yet that the title is not so transferred to men that God is robbed of the best part of his praise, since he alone is the author of what he gives by their hands. He will not let the vision stand alone: a bare vision leaves the mind in doubt, since Satan often abuses apparitions to cozen unbelievers, whereas visions truly divine the Spirit seals with a certain mark, and he sets beside this the wicked spirit that appeared to Brutus and invited him to the unhappy battle fought at the very place to which Paul was afterwards called, the cause being unlike and the Lord accordingly dealing far otherwise with his servant. He reads the sequel as a glass showing how sharply the Lord exercised their faith, since they crossed the sea in haste as though a whole nation would meet them and found none in the city to take pains with, being driven into a field to speak in an obscure corner and gaining there one woman, and she an alien; who would not have said the journey was taken in hand foolishly? Yet the Lord brings his works to pass under a base and weak appearance, that his power may shine more clearly at length.

Clarke says it is impossible to tell whether the vision came in sleep or was a representation made to the senses, and reports both the view that the guardian angel of the province appeared in human shape and the view that it was a divine communication made to the imagination in a dream; he supposes Luke joined the company at Troas, this being the first place where the historian includes himself, prefers the reading the Lord to the reading God on the ground that it was the Spirit of Jesus who had forbidden Bithynia, and says the description of Philippi as a chief city has greatly puzzled critics and commentators, reporting the defence that though another city had been made chief of that division, Philippi might have been chief two hundred and twenty years later. Wesley denies the dream flatly, observing that no dream but two is mentioned in the whole New Testament, takes the man for an angel in the Macedonian habit or using the language of the country and representing the inhabitants, and glosses the cry for help as against Satan, ignorance and sin; he remarks that Luke intimates his attendance only obliquely and never once names himself or anything he did for Christianity, though Paul speaks of him in the most honourable terms, and finds the like amiable modesty in all the sacred historians; and he settles the description of Philippi by geography, the river running between the two parts of the province.

Barnes says it is impossible to tell whether the vision came in sleep or waking, since the will of God was at different times made known both ways, reports the opinion that this was the guardian angel of the province and finds no foundation for it, notes that Macedonia was the first region in Europe in which the gospel is recorded to have been preached, and takes the call as an example to the church, similar appeals now coming from all portions of the earth; he supposes Luke joined at this point, and on the description of Philippi reports that the province had been divided into four parts, that one version reads a city of the first part, and that it has been proposed to alter the Greek since another city was made chief of that division, answering that in two hundred and twenty years Philippi may have become the most extensive and splendid, or that the phrase means simply the first city they reached. Ellicott says the vision explained to Paul all the varied promptings and drawings-back of the journey, this being the door that was to be opened, the faith of Christ passing from Asia to Europe and the cry coming to him as a call from the whole western world; he argues that since no account is given of the Evangelist's conversion he and Paul must have been known to each other already, probably at Antioch, and that the phrase the Lord had called us implies Luke was himself a preacher, rejecting the alternative that Luke incorporated a narrative by another hand; and he grants that adverse critics cite the description of Philippi as an instance of Luke's inaccuracy, notes that the Greek has no article and that the epithet first is often found on the coins of cities which were not capitals, and prefers to read the word for part as border-land, making Philippi the first city of that frontier district. Robertson reports the modern identification of the man with Luke and answers that whatever is true about Luke the narrative must not be robbed of its supernatural aspect, adds that Paul had twice been rebuffed and that most men would have gone home, that the call is now positive and not negative, and that Paul's visions always came at real crises of his life; he argues from the plural being dropped when Paul leaves the city and resumed when he returns that Luke was in the party and that a writer of such literary skill is not copying a document in a blundering way, presses the participle rendered concluding as a striking word meaning to knit together and so to infer and a good illustration of the proper use of reason alongside revelation, and describes the colony planted at Philippi with all the privileges of Roman citizenship.

debates: Whether the vision was a dream: Barnes and Clarke hold it impossible to tell, Wesley denies it flatly since only two dreams are named in the New Testament, and Calvin rests on the text, which says only that it came in the night

Who the man of Macedonia was: Barnes reports and rejects the guardian angel of the province, Clarke reports both that and a communication to the imagination, Wesley makes him an angel in the Macedonian habit, and Robertson reports the identification with Luke while insisting the narrative must not be robbed of its supernatural aspect

When and how Luke joined the party: Clarke and Barnes suppose at Troas, Ellicott argues from the silence about his conversion that he and Paul were already acquainted at Antioch and that he was himself a preacher, and Robertson argues from the dropping and resuming of the plural that Luke is in the party and is not copying a document

Whether Philippi may be called a chief city: Barnes reports the proposal to alter the Greek and answers from the lapse of two hundred and twenty years or from the order of their travels, Clarke reports the same defence, Ellicott prefers to read the word for part as border-land, and Wesley settles it by the river that divided the province
outliers: Calvin's parallel of the wicked spirit that appeared to Brutus, inviting him to the unhappy battle fought at the very place to which Paul was afterwards called
Calvin's reading of the outcome as a glass: one woman, and she an alien, gained in an obscure corner, so that who would not have said the journey was taken in hand foolishly?

Robertson's summary that it was the cry of Europe for Christ, and his portrait of Paul as a new Alexander come from Asia to conquer Europe and a new Caesar building on the work of Alexander and Caesar
Robertson's list of the colony's privileges, freedom from scourging, freedom from arrest save in extreme cases, and the right of appeal to the emperor
Robertson's remark that Luke has a true feeling for the sea, and his note that the phrase for a straight course is a nautical term for sailing before the wind
Wesley's observation on the amiable modesty of all the sacred historians, who never record what they themselves did
Ellicott on Samothrace as a chief seat of the cultus of the Cabiri, and on the name Neapolis surviving both in Naples and in the modern name of Sychem

13.pericope_label: The place of prayer by the river, the opening of Lydia’s heart, and the baptism of her household

schools.summary: Gill leaves open whether Lydia was Jewess or Gentile, since the name will not determine it: she may have been called after the region in which her native city stood, a Roman poet uses the name, and it may also be a Jewish one; he supposes the baptism was performed in the very river beside which the place of prayer stood. Calvin makes the meeting by the river a matter of danger rather than convenience, since their religion was then everywhere most odious and it was not lawful for them to assemble publicly in a Roman colony, so they withdrew into a secret corner where they could not be espied, and even that was grudged them, God teaching by their example what account we ought to make of the profession of faith, that we do not forsake it for fear of envy or of dangers. On the opened heart he observes that Luke does not assign her aptness to being of quicker intellect than the others, nor to any preparation of her own, but says simply that the Lord opened her heart, and that though he had just commended her godliness he shows she could not comprehend the doctrine of the gospel save through the illumination of the Spirit. On the household he says nothing of infants and draws a rule instead, that Lydia consecrated her family to God and that all the godly ought to desire those under them to be partakers of the same faith, so that every one of the faithful should study to order his house that it may be an image of the Church; and looking back over the whole he says that if a few women only had heard, this had been to enter as it were by a strait chink, yet from that one small graft there sprang afterwards a noble Church.

Clarke takes the name Lydia from the country, notes that the women of that region were celebrated for their purple manufactures, and reads the opened heart the other way about from Calvin: as she was a sincere worshipper she was already prepared to receive the truths spoken, and as she was faithful to the grace received God gave her more, so that it is wrong to suppose she had not received a measure of the light of God before this time; he also gives her words a distinctive sense, that her present reception of the gospel is offered as proof that she had been faithful to the light already imparted and would be as faithful to this new grace. Wesley notes that the Greek word for opening properly refers to the eyes, that the heart has its eyes, that these are closed by nature and that to open them is the peculiar work of God; he asks on the household who can believe that in so many families there was no infant, or that Jews so long accustomed to circumcise their children would not now devote them to God by baptism; and he notes that the apostles did not immediately comply with her invitation, lest any should imagine they sought their own profit by coming into Macedonia.

Barnes explains that purple was a most valuable colour obtained from shell-fish and chiefly worn by princes and the rich, so that the traffic might be very profitable, takes Lydia for a proselyte, and calls the baptism of her household a strong presumptive proof of household baptism, since her believing is particularly mentioned while theirs is not intimated and it is manifestly implied that they were baptized because she believed, the whole being the offering of her family to the Lord. Ellicott renders the phrase for the meeting-place as a place where an oratory was established, the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew house of prayer, and explains that where the Jews had no synagogue, as in a military station they were not likely to have, they frequented river-banks, which made ablutions easy, and often obtained ground assigned them outside the walls, citing a Roman satirist who noted the practice as an instance of the decay of the old faith; he takes the name from the country, adding that slaves and freedwomen commonly bore such names, notes that inscriptions attest a guild of purple-sellers at her native city, and answers the argument from the household baptism that this is to read a great deal between the lines, the utmost that can be said being that the language does not exclude infants, since the practice rests on firmer grounds than a precarious induction from a few ambiguous passages and there is no evidence here that she had children or even that she was married, the household perhaps being the female slaves and freedwomen she employed. Robertson gives the same account of the open-air enclosure near water for ceremonial ablutions and notes the word is used for a place of prayer by heathen writers too; he takes the name from the country, notes the guild of dyers attested by inscriptions and the great demand for the fabric for the official toga at Rome and in the colonies, judges Lydia a woman of some means to carry on such an enterprise from her native city, and quotes the objection that the Greek word for household may mean her servants or work-people, adding that in the household baptisms one sees infants or not according to his predilections.

Chrysostom marks that the place of prayer was set apart out of the city and by a river, and that the sabbath was chosen when a multitude would be likely to come together; he praises the calling itself, that here was a woman, and she of low condition, and from her trade too, yet a woman of elevated mind, and that the fact of God's calling her bears testimony to her; and he marks the wisdom of her words, that nothing could be more persuasive than if ye have judged me faithful, since she did not request or entreat simply but left the apostles to decide and yet exceedingly forced them, and did not dare to invite them before this.

debates: Whether the household baptism proves infant baptism: Barnes calls it a strong presumptive proof and Wesley asks who can believe there was no infant in so many families, while Ellicott answers that the utmost that can be said is that the language does not exclude infants, and Robertson observes that one sees infants there or not according to his predilections

What it means that the Lord opened her heart: Calvin denies any preparation or quickness of her own and rests everything on the illumination of the Spirit, while Clarke holds that as a sincere worshipper she was already prepared and was given more grace because faithful to what she had, so that it is wrong to suppose she had no light before

Why they met by the river: Ellicott and Robertson make it convenience, the want of a synagogue and the need of water for ablutions, while Calvin makes it danger, since public assembly was not lawful in a Roman colony and even the secret corner was grudged them

Whether Lydia's name was her own or her country's: Gill leaves it open and notes it may be Jewish, while Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson take it from the region, Ellicott adding that slaves and freedwomen commonly bore such names

What her words mean: Chrysostom takes them as the height of persuasion, leaving the apostles to judge while exceedingly forcing them, where Clarke takes them as an argument from her past fidelity to the light already given
outliers: Chrysostom's opening remark, see again Paul judaizing, and his note that the Jews set apart such a place because as Jews they were more corporeal
Ellicott's quotation of the Roman satirist on groves and streams that were once sacred ground being now let out to Jews
Robertson's line that in the household baptisms one sees infants or not according to his predilections or preferences
Robertson's note that the fabric was used on the official toga at Rome and in the colonies, so that we still speak of royal purple

Calvin's rule that every one of the faithful should so order his house that it may be an image of the Church, and that he is unworthy to be numbered among the children of God who would reign in his own house and let none there give place to Christ
Calvin's image of entering by a strait chink, and of a noble Church springing afterwards from that one small graft
Wesley's observation that the heart has its eyes, closed by nature, and that to open them is the peculiar work of God

16.pericope_label: The slave girl with a spirit of divination, her testimony, and her deliverance

schools.summary: Gill says that to use the phrase of the act of prayer is a mere Anglicism, unknown to the eastern writers, and insists on the prayer-house, since the damsel followed them for many days and knew by their going there what they were; he says she was suffered to continue so long that the expulsion of the spirit might be the more manifest, the apostles having no need of such a testimony. Calvin holds that Luke follows the common custom of speaking about the spirit of Python and so exhibits the error of the common people, the poets having feigned that the serpent was slain by the dart of Phoebus and a further fiction having grown from it; he supposes Paul at first neglected the crying, hoping it would vanish of itself, but that the continual repetition wearied him, since long dissembling would have made Satan more insolent, and adds a caution that Paul could not have commanded rashly, the word being foolish and vain without the commandment of God, which must be noted lest any condemn him of too great hastiness; he also reads the passage as recording the increase of the Church, since it is easily gathered from the text that many were brought into the faith, and observes that when Satan had done his worst there was still a body of the Church gathered before the apostles departed.

Henry calls her a pythoness, possessed with such a spirit of divination as that by which the oracles of Apollo at Delphi were delivered, actuated by an evil spirit which dictated ambiguous answers that gratified the vain desire of knowing things to come and often deceived; in those times of ignorance and idolatry the devil by divine permission led men captive at his will, and could not have gained such adoration from them as he had if he had not pretended to give them oracles, since by both his usurpation is maintained as the god of this world; and he notes that many consulted her for the discovery of robberies and the finding of things lost.

Clarke reports that several manuscripts add the article to the word for the place of prayer, which makes the place emphatic and confirms that the oratory and not the act is meant; he tells the story of the serpent slain by Apollo, from which the god and his prophetesses took their name, and adds that all who could predict future events, or pretended to, were said to be influenced by that spirit; he finds a deep design in the damsel's cry, that the testimony was every syllable true and yet calculated to ruin the apostles, since the Jewish law abhorred all dealings with familiar spirits, so that the Jews would conclude they were in compact with demons and their miracles wrought by magic; and he observes that Paul turned to the spirit and not to the woman, she being only the organ by which it acted, arguing that every circumstance proves a real possession, since Luke's training as a physician equipped him to detect imposture and he finds none, speaking of the spirit and the damsel as distinct persons. Wesley says only that it was a great truth, but that Paul neither needed nor would accept such testimony.

Barnes tells the story of the serpent slain by Apollo and describes the almost universal worship of the god, offers three conjectures why the damsel cried after them and prefers the last, that she hoped for a reward, or feared expulsion and hoped to conciliate them, or more probably saw evident tokens that their doctrine would prevail and hoped by proclaiming it to gain more authority and a higher reputation for inspiration; and he lists five grounds of Paul's grief, among them that the woman's state was one of bondage and delusion and that the system behind it held a large part of the pagan world. Ellicott concedes that the Greek has no article for the place of prayer, so far favouring the received rendering, but answers that the word for church is likewise used without one and that we say going to church without it; he makes the serpent the symbol of wisdom worshipped at Delphi, refuses to read the cry merely as a demon mocking, since it shows the same symptom of a divided consciousness and spoke of a mind longing for deliverance and peace, the girl seeing in the preachers those able to deliver her and as unlike as possible to the masters who traded on her maddened misery; and he asks whether it was not right for Paul to do as his Master had done and restore the woman to her true self, refusing to think she was afterwards left to drift back into unbelief. Robertson observes that a later writer applied the term to ventriloquists, that the Greek Old Testament uses it of those with familiar spirits, that the word for soothsaying is the old heathen term for acting the seer and is akin to the verb meaning to be mad, and that Luke certainly does not mean to credit Apollo with a real existence; he notes that pagan inscriptions use the same title for the Supreme Being, that the Greek has a way of salvation without the article since there were many ways offered to men then as now, that Paul, like his Master, distinguished between the demon and the individual, and that the cure was instantaneous.

debates: Whether the phrase means the act of prayer or the place: Gill calls the first a mere Anglicism unknown to eastern writers, Clarke reports manuscripts adding the article to make the place emphatic, and Ellicott concedes the Greek has none but answers from the parallel use of the word for church

Why the damsel cried after them: Barnes offers three conjectures and prefers the hope of authority and reputation, Clarke finds a deep design of the spirit to ruin their credit with Jews who abhorred familiar spirits, Ellicott hears a divided consciousness and a mind longing for deliverance, and Wesley says only that it was a truth Paul neither needed nor would accept

Whether the possession was real: Clarke argues every circumstance proves it and that Luke's medical training would have detected imposture, while Robertson notes the term was applied to ventriloquists and used in the Greek Old Testament of those with familiar spirits, insisting Luke does not credit Apollo with a real existence, and Calvin says Luke follows the common speech and so exhibits the error of the common people

Why Paul bore it so long and then acted: Gill says she was suffered so the expulsion might be more manifest, Calvin that Paul hoped it would vanish but could not dissemble longer without making Satan insolent, and could not have commanded at all without the commandment of God, and Robertson that Paul wanted no testimony from such a source
outliers: Henry's account of the oracles, that the devil could not have gained such adoration had he not pretended to give men oracles, and that many consulted her for the discovery of robberies and the finding of things lost
Robertson's note that the word for soothsaying is akin to the verb meaning to be mad, like the howling dervishes of later times
Robertson's observation that the Greek has a way of salvation without the article, there being many ways of salvation offered to men then as now
Clarke's argument from Luke's education as a physician, which gave him advantages to detect imposture of this kind, and his finding none here
Ellicott's hope that the delivered girl found shelter and comfort at the hands of the women who laboured with the Apostle
Calvin's observation that when Satan had done his worst there was still a body of the Church gathered before the apostles departed

19.pericope_label: The masters lose their gain, the apostles are accused as Jews, beaten and put in the stocks

schools.summary: Gill notes that the masters could see the girl was sedate and composed, no longer wild and frantic as while the spirit possessed her, that the word for magistrates properly signifies military captains, and reports an authority for ten magistrates being chosen yearly; he takes the customs complained of to be the doctrine of salvation by Christ, whom they took for a new deity, and supposes the crowd was spirited up by the girl's owners and encouraged by the rulers. Calvin sees the same devil at work in both scenes, since he who had lately flattered Paul by the mouth of the maid now drives her masters into fury, having changed his coat to play a tragedy where fair speech and flattery could not speed; he holds that though the heat of zeal by which Paul was provoked raised the whirlwind of persecution he is not therefore to be blamed, nor did it repent him of the miracle, whereby we are taught not rashly to condemn things well done. He calls the accusation craftily composed, since on the one side they pretend the name of the Romans, than which nothing was more favourable, and on the other purchase hatred by naming the Jews, whose name was then infamous, a Roman being free to sacrifice in any country where there were idols; and on the appeal to custom he turns the passage against his own opponents, who lean upon a prejudice lest the cause come to be disputed, saying that a thing was decreed in a General Council, or is too ancient and common an opinion to be questioned, or has been approved by long usage, all of which tend only to rob the Word of God of authority, boasting of men's decrees while leaving no place for the laws of God.

Clarke explains that the girl was maintained by men who received a fee from everyone whose fortune she told or whose stolen goods she discovered, and adds that she herself continued a heathen, since we do not hear a word of her conversion, making that silence an argument that the possession had been real, for had she been converted and baptized and joined to the apostles there would have been some show of reason for denying it. He makes the magistrates commanders of the army, who in a Roman colony possessed the sovereign authority, supplies the ground of the charge from the Roman side, that they were very jealous of their national worship, quoting a poet and his commentator to prove it, notes that the Jews were limited to forty stripes save one while the Romans had no such law so that the apostles had the fullest measure, and describes the stocks as two pieces of wood pierced with holes at different distances, so that the legs might be separated to a great extent and extreme pain produced. Wesley calls the magistrates the supreme magistrates of the city, exercising both military and civil authority, says the Jews were a nation peculiarly despised by the Romans, and puts the charge about customs the other way about: the world has received all the rules and doctrines of all the philosophers that ever were, but gospel truth has something in it peculiarly intolerable to the world; he supposes either that they did not immediately say they were Romans or that in the tumult it was not regarded, and that the charge to the jailer was perhaps rather to quiet the people than because the magistrates thought them criminal.

Barnes observes that instead of regarding the act as proof of divine power the masters were intent only on their profits, and finds in their indignation a remarkable illustration of the fixedness with which men regard wealth and of the fact that any interposition destroying their hopes of gain fills them with wrath; he calls the accusation cunning and artful, since they cared nothing for the religion either of Rome or of the Jews, notes how conscientious they all at once became about the violation of the laws, observes that the beating was done in a popular tumult without even the form of law and in violation of the privileges of a Roman citizen, and that the Jews were limited to forty stripes save one while the Romans were unrestricted. Ellicott finds something like a prophetic significance in the use at this stage of the very word which was the key to nearly all the persecutions the early believers suffered, since men could tolerate varieties of worship or the speculations of philosophers but were roused to madness by whatever threatened their business; he recalls that the decree banishing the Jews from Rome would be known at Philippi and would give the charge special force, that the inhabitants of a colony could claim the title of Roman citizens as those of a merely Greek city could not, and that the word for magistrates is used with Luke's usual accuracy of the praetors who formed the executive of a colony; he raises the question why Paul did not then claim his citizenship and answers that some suppose the violence of the mob made it impossible for the claim to be heard and others have questioned its truthfulness, but that the more natural supposition is that he would not assert a right securing exemption for himself alone; and he describes the darkness and foulness of such a dungeon from prisons of the empire still to be seen. Robertson quotes another that the most sensitive part of civilised man is the pocket, and a second that the two most important social revolutions worked by Christianity have been the elevation of woman and the abolition of slavery, both illustrated in this chapter; he marks the sharp contrast between being Jews in one verse and being Romans in the next, calls the pose of patriotism all sound and fury since it is love of money that moves these masters, adds that no Roman magistrate would pass on abstract theological questions but only on a breach of the peace, gives the technical name of the magistrates and observes that as they represented consuls they were attended by lictors bearing rods, and describes the inner prison as a veritable dungeon with no light or air save what came through the door when open.

debates: Why the masters were enraged: Barnes makes it an illustration of the fixedness with which men regard wealth, Ellicott finds prophetic significance in the word that was the key to nearly all the early persecutions, and Robertson quotes the verdict that the most sensitive part of civilised man is the pocket

How the accusation was framed: Calvin calls it craftily composed, pretending the favourable Roman name while purchasing hatred by the infamous Jewish one, Robertson calls the pose of patriotism all sound and fury, Barnes calls it cunning and artful, and Ellicott recalls the decree banishing the Jews from Rome
Whether the girl was converted: Clarke says flatly that she continued a heathen, no word of her conversion being heard, and makes that silence an argument that the possession had been real

Why Paul did not claim his citizenship then: Ellicott canvasses the violence of the mob and the doubts cast on the claim's truthfulness, and prefers that Paul would not assert a right securing exemption for himself alone, while Wesley supposes either that they did not say it or that it went unregarded in the tumult

Who the magistrates were: Gill takes the word for military captains yet identifies them with the ten annual magistrates, Clarke makes them commanders of the army holding sovereign authority in a colony, and Ellicott and Robertson identify them as the praetors or duumvirs of the colony, attended by lictors with rods
outliers: Robertson's quotation that the two most important social revolutions worked by Christianity have been the elevation of woman and the abolition of slavery, both illustrated in this chapter
Ellicott's observation that men could tolerate varieties of worship or the speculations of philosophers but were roused to madness by what threatened their business
Calvin's comparison of the appeal to ancient custom with the appeals of his own opponents to General Councils and immemorial usage, which serve only to rob the Word of God of authority
Wesley's remark that the world has received the doctrines of all the philosophers that ever were, but that gospel truth has something in it peculiarly intolerable to the world
Clarke's account of the stocks, pierced with holes at different distances so that the legs might be separated to a great extent, with the quotation from a Christian poet on the torments of a martyr
Calvin's judgment that Paul is not to be blamed though his zeal raised the whirlwind of persecution, and that we must not rashly condemn things which are well done
Ellicott's note that the title of the magistrates survived into the eighteenth century in an Italian term for the prefect of Messina

25.pericope_label: Prayer and singing at midnight, the earthquake, and the jailer’s drawn sword

schools.summary: Gill says they prayed for themselves and for support under their afflictions, for their enemies and particularly for the jailer who had used them so ill, and for the churches of Christ; he denies flatly that the earthquake arose from natural causes, from wind pent up in the earth, and makes it rise from the prayers and praises of the saints going up to heaven, the effects that followed showing it supernatural; and he supposes the jailer was wakened less by their voices than by the uncommon motion of the earth. Calvin observes that the Lord could have loosed the fetters and opened the gates without an earthquake, but that the addition served not a little to confirm them, seeing that for their sakes he shook both the air and the earth, and that it was requisite besides that the keeper of the prison and the rest should feel the presence of God, lest they should think the miracle came by chance; he adds that the Lord then showed a token of his power profitable for all ages. On the drawn sword he alone turns the question round and asks why Paul hindered the jailer at all, since it had been a foolish answer to say the doors opened of their own accord, and since the man's death might have opened a way of escape, so that Paul seems by preventing it to refuse the deliverance God had offered.

Henry frames the whole scene as the designs of the persecutors baffled and broken: they meant to dishearten and discourage the preachers of the gospel and to make them weary of their work, and here we find them both hearty and heartened, never were poor prisoners so truly cheerful nor so far from laying their hard usage to heart; he recalls that the praetors had rods carried before them and axes bound upon them, and that the apostles had felt the smart of those rods, the ploughers having ploughed upon their backs and made long furrows.

Clarke says the two were undismayed and even happy in their sufferings, so fully satisfied that they were right and had done their duty that there was no room for regret or self-reproach, and that they prayed first for grace to support them and for the pardon and salvation of their persecutors and then sang praises to God who had accounted them worthy to suffer shame, and sang so loud and heartily that the prisoners heard them though they were in the inner prison. On the earthquake he keeps the miracle but puts the wonder elsewhere, that God's providence so conducted everything that not one prisoner escaped though the doors were open and the bolts off, and he reads the event symbolically, that the religion they preached shakes and terrifies the guilty while proclaiming deliverance to the captives and the opening of the prison to them that are bound. On the drawn sword he says every jailer was made responsible under the same penalty as his prisoner, so that he chose to die by his own hand rather than another's, the custom being applauded by the philosophers and sanctioned by some of their greatest men. Wesley says only that they sang notwithstanding weariness, hunger, stripes and blood, and that the prisoners heard a song to which they were not accustomed.

Barnes takes the plainer view of the vigil, that their painful posture and the smart of the recent scourging prevented sleep, but that though they had no repose they had a quiet conscience and the supports of religion, and that a Christian may find more true joy in a prison than the monarch on his throne, prayer and praise not being common in a prison. He calls the loosing of every one's bands evidently a miracle and rejects the suggestion that the chains were dissolved by electric fluid, the narrative giving no account of any such thing; and on the drawn sword he explains that a jailer was held responsible for the safe keeping of his prisoners and subject to the punishment due to them, and that suicide was common and approved among Greeks and Romans when a man was encompassed with dangers, men of the first rank having fallen on their own swords and many having done so at this very place after the great battle fought there. Ellicott renders the Greek as expressing one act rather than two, praying they were singing hymns, adds that the act was habitual and would not be intermitted even when they were fastened so that they could not kneel, and suggests the hymn may have been one of the prayer-psalms of David or one of those later described by a Roman governor in which men offered adoration to Christ as God, quoting an early Latin father to the martyrs, that the leg feels not the stocks when the mind is in heaven. He says the region and the time were both conspicuous for such convulsions, that Luke apparently reads the fact not as in itself miraculous but as leading to a display of supernatural calmness and so to the jailer's conversion, and that since the chains were fastened to rings or staples in the wall a great shock would loosen the stones; and he presses hardest the local predisposition to suicide, the town having been conspicuous after the great battle for those who preferred death to the loss of freedom, an act looked on as heroic and naturally contagious. Robertson agrees that the Greek blends petition and praise in one act, supposes portions of the Psalms with occasional original outbursts of praise, notes that the verb for the prisoners' listening is a rare one meaning to listen with pleasure as to a recitation or music, supposes the prison excavated from rock in the hillside so that the shock would slip the bars and shake the chains from the walls, and puts the jailer's impulse in a word, that the Stoic philosophy had made suicide popular as the escape from trouble.

Chrysostom asks what could equal these souls: they had been scourged and had received many stripes, had been misused, were in peril of their lives, were thrust into the inner prison and set fast in the stocks, and for all this did not suffer themselves to sleep but kept vigil all the night; he asks whether we mark what a blessing tribulation is, since we in our soft beds, with none to be afraid of, pass the whole night in sleep, and observes that neither the tyranny of sleep could overpower them, nor the smart of pain bow them, nor the fear of evil cast them into helpless dejection, these being the very things that made them wakeful and filled them with exceeding delight.

debates: Whether the earthquake and the loosing of the bands were miraculous: Gill denies natural causes outright and Barnes calls the loosing evidently a miracle, while Ellicott says Luke does not read the fact as in itself miraculous and explains the chains from rings loosened in the wall, Robertson from a prison cut in rock, and Calvin holds God could have done it without the earthquake, which was added for confirmation and to prevent the bystanders thinking it chance
Why they were awake and singing: Chrysostom makes the tribulation itself the cause and the source of their delight, where Barnes ascribes the wakefulness to pain and a quiet conscience

What the singing was: Ellicott and Robertson agree the Greek makes praying and singing one act, Ellicott suggesting a prayer-psalm or an early hymn offering adoration to Christ as God, Robertson portions of the Psalms with original outbursts

Why the jailer drew his sword, and why Paul hindered him: Clarke, Barnes and Ellicott explain the jailer's liability and the local prestige of suicide after the great battle fought at Philippi, and Robertson credits the Stoic philosophy, while Calvin alone asks why Paul prevented a death that might have opened a way of escape, so seeming to refuse the deliverance God had offered
outliers: Chrysostom's contrast, that we in our soft beds with none to be afraid of pass the whole night in sleep, and his question whether we mark what a blessing tribulation is
Barnes's judgment that a Christian may find more true joy in a prison than the monarch on his throne
Ellicott's quotation from an early Latin father to the martyrs, that the leg feels not the stocks when the mind is in heaven
Ellicott's suggestion that the hymn may have been one of those a Roman governor later described, in which men offered adoration to Christ as God
Robertson's note that the verb for the prisoners' listening means to listen with pleasure, as to a recitation or music
Barnes's rejection of the suggestion that the prisoners' chains were dissolved by electric fluid
Clarke's symbolic reading, that the religion they preached shakes and terrifies the guilty while proclaiming deliverance to the captives
Henry's image of the praetors' rods, the ploughers having ploughed upon the apostles' backs and made long furrows

28.pericope_label: Do thyself no harm, the jailer’s question, and the answer to believe

schools.summary: Gill says Paul knew what the man was about by divine revelation, since from the innermost prison and in a dark dungeon he could not have seen him unless the opened doors let in light enough, and adds that he may have known in the same way what designs of grace God had toward the man and his family; he draws the contrast that while the jailer was going about a work of darkness he was in no concern for a light and called for one only when delivered from the snare; and he guards the apostles' answer, that a bare historical faith will not serve, since there may be such a faith and no salvation, but that he must look to Christ alone for life and salvation, rely on him and commit the care of his immortal soul to him. Calvin observes what a good thing it is for men to be thrown down from their pride, since one hardened in his superstitions might with a lofty stomach have despised whatever they said, whom he had disgracefully thrust into the innermost prison, whereas fear now makes him apt to be taught and gentle; he marks that the man asks counsel in such a way as to show he will obey, where the wicked often tremble at wonders for a time and are then made more obstinate, as Pharaoh was; and he calls the answer a short and, to look to, a cold and hungry definition of salvation, and yet perfect, since Christ alone has all the parts of blessedness and eternal life included in him and is the only mark at which faith must aim, so that men's minds do nothing but wander when they turn aside from him.

Clarke says that as it was now midnight Paul must have had a divine intimation of what the jailer was going to do; he explains the call for lights, that the man wanted to see whether Paul's words were true, since on that his own safety depended, and adds in passing that it does not appear he had exceeded his orders in his treatment of the apostles; he argues that since not one prisoner had escaped the jailer could not think himself in danger of losing his life, so that his question cannot have been about personal safety, and that he must have known the apostles had been preaching what they called the doctrine of salvation; and on the answer he says only that the man was to receive the religion of Christ which they preached and let his household receive it also. Wesley agrees that Paul knew by an immediate notice from God, which is by no means incredible, and explains the loud voice by earnestness and by the distance between them; he states the principle that though the Christian faith opens the prospect into another life it absolutely forbids and effectually prevents a man's discharging himself from this; he notes that the jailer did not style them Sirs the day before, and makes his question arise from the guilt he felt and the vengeance he feared, God having set his sins in array before him; and he adds that they believed and were saved.

Barnes makes the words the standing command of religion, forbidding men to do themselves harm not only by the sword or the halter but by intemperance and dissipation, since in all cases Christianity seeks the true welfare of man; he ascribes the jailer's trembling to the earthquake, to amazement that the prisoners were still there, and to confusion at the calmness of Paul and Silas, takes the falling down for an act of profound reverence, argues that since the prisoners were all safe he could scarcely consider himself exposed to punishment by the Romans and that the apostles' answer would have been no remedy for such a danger in any case, and marks what they did not say, that they did not direct him to use the means of grace, to pray, or to keep seeking, nor advise him to delay or wait for mercy, but told him to believe at once, presuming he would understand what believing was and commanding him to do the thing. Ellicott hears in Paul's cry the love and sympathy that burnt in his heart, for whom the suicide others would have admired, or at least have thought of without horror, would have been the most terrible of all forms of death, and who could not bear that even the gaoler who had thrust him into the dungeon should so perish in his despair; he notes that the word used is not the one for lamps, so that these were probably torches, and that the man leapt with one in his hand into the darkness of the subterranean dungeon; he asks whether the jailer was thinking of temporal safety or whether there had come upon him, in that suicidal agony, the sense of an inward misery and shame, a horror of great darkness, and thinks the latter every way most probable, adding that the very circumstances which had brought Paul to the prison had pointed him out as proclaiming the way of salvation, so that the witness of the possessed girl was not altogether fruitless; and he notes that the plural in the answer shows Paul was not the only teacher, and that the Greek sets the respectful title the man had used against the one Lord they name. Robertson takes the prohibition as forbidding the man to begin the act, makes the falling down an act of worship as Cornelius before Peter, observes that he left the other prisoners inside and that there may have been superstition behind his fear but there was evident sincerity, and says that what he meant by being saved was certainly more than escape from peril.

debates: How Paul knew what the jailer was about: Gill, Clarke and Wesley all make it a divine intimation, since it was midnight and Paul was in the inner dungeon, Wesley calling such immediate notice by no means incredible and Gill extending it to the designs of grace toward the man's family

What the jailer meant by being saved: Barnes and Clarke argue from the prisoners' remaining that he cannot have meant danger from Rome, Ellicott prefers an inward misery and a horror of great darkness, Robertson says certainly more than escape from peril, and Wesley makes it the guilt he felt and the vengeance he feared

Whether the answer was too short: Calvin calls it a cold and hungry definition to look at and yet perfect, Barnes marks that they did not send him to means or prayer or delay but bade him believe at once, and Gill guards it against a bare historical faith

What moved the jailer: Calvin contrasts him with Pharaoh, since the wicked often tremble at wonders and are then hardened, while here fear made him apt to be taught; Barnes ascribes it to the earthquake and the calmness of the prisoners; Clarke says he called for a light to see whether Paul's words were true, his own safety depending on it
outliers: Ellicott's judgment that for Paul the suicide which others would have admired would have been the most terrible of all forms of death, and that he could not bear that even his own gaoler should perish in his despair
Ellicott's link back to the earlier scene, that the witness of the possessed girl proclaiming the way of salvation was thus not altogether fruitless
Ellicott's note that the plural answer shows Silas also taught, and that the Greek sets the jailer's respectful Sirs against the one Lord they name
Barnes's extension of the words to forbid harm by intemperance and dissipation as well as by the sword and the halter
Wesley's rule that the Christian faith opens the prospect into another life yet absolutely forbids and effectually prevents a man's discharging himself from this
Gill's observation that the man was in no concern for a light while going about a work of darkness, and called for one only when delivered from the snare
Clarke's aside that it does not appear the jailer had exceeded his orders in his treatment of the apostles

32.pericope_label: The word spoken to the household, the baptism and the washing of the stripes, and the order of release

schools.summary: Gill describes the word of the Lord as the gospel, called the word of salvation and of reconciliation and of life, since it publishes salvation by Christ and peace by his blood, and says the apostles opened and explained it to the jailer for his comfort; he supposes the baptism took place either in the pool in the prison or in the river near the city. Calvin commends the godly zeal by which the jailer consecrated his whole house to the Lord, wherein the grace of God appears in bringing the whole family to a godly consent, and marks the notable exchange, that the man who was lately about to murder himself because he thought his prisoners escaped now lays aside all fear and brings them home of his own accord, which shows how faith animates those to behave stoutly who before had no heart; on the meal he says the outward profession was commended before and the inward fruit now, since in lodging them and not fearing punishment, entertaining them otherwise than the magistrate had enjoined, he testified that his faith was not idle, and that the joy Luke speaks of is a singular good thing which every man has from his faith, there being no greater torment than an evil conscience, so that unbelievers, having no peace with God, must needs quake and tremble; and on the release he says only that the judges were brought to repentance of their own accord, as commonly falls out when a sedition has been raised.

Henry says the magistrates gave the order so early, as soon as it was day, which intimates either that they were sensible the terrific earthquake at midnight was intended to plead the cause of their prisoners or that their consciences had smitten them for what they had done and made them uneasy; and he draws the contrast that while the persecuted were singing in the stocks the persecutors were full of tossings to and fro upon their beds through anguish of mind, complaining more of the lashes of their consciences than the prisoners did of the lashes on their backs, and being more in haste to give them a discharge than the prisoners were to petition for one.

Clarke argues from the word rendered straightway that there can have been no immersion, since the dead of night, the general agitation, the necessity of dispatch and the words of the text all disprove it, so that the apostles must have had another method of administering baptism; and he adds that to wash the blood from the wounds would not require putting the men into a pool or bath, as some have ridiculously imagined. He puts the meal as an exchange, that as the apostles were the instruments of health to the jailer's soul he became the instrument of health to their bodies, genuine faith being always accompanied with benevolence and humanity; and on the release he says we cannot tell why the magistrates dismissed them, unless we receive the reading of one manuscript which adds that they came together into the court and, remembering the earthquake that had happened, were afraid. Wesley observes that the apostles had not the power of working miraculous cures when they pleased, either on themselves or their dearest friends, and that it was not expedient they should, since it would have frustrated many wise designs of God which were answered by their sufferings; he sums the jailer's change in four words, that faith makes a man joyful, prudent, liberal; and he supposes the praetors were terrified by the earthquake, noting how different the message was from the charge given a few hours before, and what an ease of mind to the jailer.

Barnes says the apostles instructed the house, old and young, in the doctrines of religion and in the nature of the ordinances, and then baptized the whole family; he observes that though they had the gift of miracles they did not exercise it on their own sufferings, restoring others and not themselves, and marks the effect of religion in producing humanity and tenderness, since the same man who a few hours before had thrust them into the inner prison and made them fast in the stocks, with no concern for their wounds, made an act of humanity one of his first acts once converted; he contrasts the family as it was when Paul was thrust into prison with the scene when he was brought out as an honoured guest at the very table of the renovated jailer, and says an earthquake is always fitted to alarm the guilty and was among the Romans regarded as an omen of the anger of the gods. Ellicott argues that belief in Christ, unless it were to be a mere formula repeated as a charm, required explanation, so that the title itself, the acts and words that showed Jesus was the Christ, his life and death and resurrection, forgiveness of sins and communion with him, and the outward signs appointed as witnesses of those truths must all have been included in the word preached to that congregation so strangely assembled between midnight and dawn, even this gaoler having to be a catechumen before he was baptised; he holds that no certain answer can be given between immersion and affusion, but that a public prison was likely enough to contain a bath or pool where the former would be feasible; he sets the two washings in suggestive juxtaposition, the one testifying of the jailer's repentance and kindly reverence, the other administered as the washing of regeneration, so that he too was cleansed from wounds worse than any the rods had made; he reckons that the two had probably fasted nearly twenty-four hours, and that the absence of the specific term for breaking bread excludes the idea of a eucharist in the later sense; and on the release he thinks it more probable that the magistrates felt they had acted hastily in ordering punishment without any regular trial or inquiry, and wanted to wash their hands of the business as quietly as possible. Robertson calls the night's teaching a remarkable service with keenest attention, the jailer attending with his warden, his slaves and his household, canvasses for the baptism the tank in which the jailer had bathed them, the rectangular basin in the court for receiving rain, and a swimming bath within the walls, quoting another that the water was perhaps in the court of the house and the baptism that of immersion, which formed an essential part of the symbolism of the act; and on the release he reports the manuscript reading about the earthquake and allows the earthquake, the influence of Lydia and a belated sense of justice together.

debates: Whether the baptism was by immersion: Clarke argues from the word rendered straightway and from the hour and the haste that it cannot have been, Ellicott holds no certain answer can be given though a prison bath would make it feasible, and Robertson canvasses three possible basins and quotes another for immersion as an essential part of the symbolism

Why the magistrates changed their minds: Henry offers the earthquake or their consciences, Barnes the earthquake as a Roman omen of divine anger, Clarke and Robertson report a manuscript that says they remembered it and were afraid, Ellicott prefers an uneasy sense of having punished without trial, and Calvin says only that it is what commonly follows a sedition

Whether the apostles could have healed themselves: Barnes and Wesley agree that they had the gift but did not exercise it on their own sufferings, Wesley adding that it was not expedient, since it would have frustrated wise designs of God answered by their sufferings

What the word of the Lord contained: Ellicott lists the whole substance and says even this gaoler had to be a catechumen before baptism, Barnes has them instructed in the doctrines and the ordinances, and Robertson calls it a service of the keenest attention
outliers: Henry's picture of the persecutors full of tossings to and fro upon their beds, complaining more of the lashes of their consciences than the prisoners did of the lashes on their backs
Barnes's contrast between the household as Paul was thrust into prison and the same household seating him as an honoured guest at the renovated jailer's table
Ellicott's reckoning that the two had probably fasted nearly twenty-four hours, and his note that the absence of the term for breaking bread excludes a eucharist in the later sense
Ellicott's pairing of the two washings, the jailer washing their stripes and they washing him in regeneration, he too being cleansed from worse wounds than the rods had made
