Calvin's notable exchange, that the man lately about to murder himself now lays aside all fear and brings his prisoners home of his own accord
Clarke's remark that washing the blood from the wounds would not require putting the men into a pool, as some have ridiculously imagined
Wesley's summary in four words, that faith makes a man joyful, prudent, liberal

36.pericope_label: Paul refuses a quiet release, the magistrates come in person, and the apostles depart

schools.summary: Gill notes that the message of release was brought by the jailer himself, whom Paul had baptized, and reported no doubt with great joy, and that the apostles went out publicly, with great honour and reputation, at the request of the very men who had put them there. Calvin is harder on the magistrates than any: they are not once moved by the other point, that they had handled innocent men cruelly without any previous inquiry, and yet that was the greater reproach, but because they did not fear that any man would punish them they were not moved by the judgment of God, and carelessly passed over the injury they had done, being afraid only of the Roman axes and of being beheaded for violating the liberty of a citizen. On the departure he says they would undoubtedly have tarried longer had they been suffered, the prayers and requests of the magistrates being imperious and armed, but that they did not neglect their necessary duty of exhorting the brethren to be constant, and that their going straight to Lydia is a token that though the church was increased that woman was still the chief even of a greater number as touching diligence in the duties of godliness, which appears the more plainly because the godly were assembled in her house.

Clarke names the two Roman laws, one forbidding a citizen to be bound and the other to be beaten with rods, adds that the liberty of a citizen was never put into the power of the lictor, and quotes the orator who said it is a transgression of the law to bind a Roman citizen and wickedness to scourge him; he adds from a manuscript a fuller apology, in which the magistrates plead that they had been ignorant the prisoners were righteous men and beg them to leave the city lest an insurrection be raised against them again; and he closes with the fruit of the visit, that the magistrates were sufficiently humbled, that the public must be satisfied of the apostles' innocence, and that great and lasting good was done, a church being founded whose members did credit to their profession. Wesley observes that Paul does not always plead this privilege, but that in a country where they were entire strangers such treatment might have brought upon them a suspicion of having been guilty of some uncommon crime and so have hindered the course of the gospel; and he says that though many circumstances invited their stay they wisely complied with the magistrates' request, that they might not seem to express any degree of obstinacy or revenge, or give any suspicion of a design to stir up the people.

Barnes names three aggravating circumstances of which Paul complains, that they had been beaten contrary to the Roman laws, that it had been done publicly so that the reparation ought to be as public, and that it had been done without a trial while they were uncondemned, so that the magistrates ought themselves to come and release them and publicly acknowledge their error; he says Paul knew the privileges of a Roman citizen and at proper times, when the interests of justice and religion required it, did not hesitate to assert them, reports that the penalty for transgressing the law was death and the confiscation of property and that an emperor deprived a city of its freedom for crucifying Roman citizens, calls the magistrates' coming a most humiliating act but in this case unavoidable since the apostles had them completely in their power, says they besought them to depart partly to save their own character and partly to prevent a further popular tumult, and infers from the change of person that Luke did not accompany Paul and Silas from the city. Ellicott recalls that the exemption of citizens from degrading punishment was the heaviest of all the charges brought against a notorious provincial governor, and that the three words by which a man claimed his citizenship acted almost like a charm in stopping the violence of provincial magistrates, adding that Paul was a citizen by birth, his father having probably been wealthy enough to buy the privilege; he judges that Paul's motive in insisting was less the satisfaction of his own honour than a desire to impress the magistrates with the wrong they had done, observes that their ignorance was no sufficient defence and that they were liable to prosecution, so that the tables were turned and the accused had become a possible accuser, notes that the jailer used the parting phrase in the fulness of its meaning and not as a mere conventional formula, and draws from the change of person that the Evangelist remained and seems to have made the city the centre of his work for many years, tracing to his influence and to Lydia's kindness the generous help afterwards sent to Paul at Thessalonica and probably at Corinth. Robertson calls the reply a marvel of brevity and energy, almost every word carrying a separate indictment of the illegality of the whole proceeding, quotes the orator that to fetter a Roman citizen was a crime, to scourge him a scandal and to slay him parricide, reports that an emperor had deprived a whole city of its freedom for crucifying a Roman citizen, says the magistrates became frightened for their own lives since the colonists would have turned against them had the facts been known, proud as they were of their citizenship, and notes that the brethren met at Lydia's house, which was now probably the meeting-place of the church.

debates: Why the privilege was pleaded now and not before: Wesley says Paul does not always plead it but that among entire strangers such treatment might have raised a suspicion of some uncommon crime and hindered the gospel, Ellicott judges his motive was less his own honour than the impression to be made on the magistrates, and Barnes says only that he asserted it at proper times

What the magistrates feared: Barnes and Robertson name the legal penalty and the anger of a colony proud of its citizenship, Ellicott that their ignorance was no defence and the accused had become a possible accuser, while Calvin says they were untouched by the greater reproach of punishing innocent men without inquiry and feared only the Roman axes

Who remained at Philippi: Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson all infer from the change of person that Luke stayed behind, Ellicott adding that he seems to have made the city the centre of his work for years and tracing to him and to Lydia the help afterwards sent to Paul

Why they complied and departed: Wesley says they did so lest they seem obstinate or vengeful or be suspected of stirring up the people, Calvin that they would have tarried longer had they been suffered but the magistrates' requests were imperious and armed, and Barnes that their purpose in the city was already accomplished
outliers: Ellicott's remark that the three words by which a man claimed his citizenship acted almost like a charm in stopping the violence of provincial magistrates

Robertson's judgment that Paul's reply is a marvel of brevity and energy, almost every word a separate indictment, with the orator's saying that to fetter a Roman citizen was a crime, to scourge him a scandal, to slay him parricide
The report in Barnes and Robertson that an emperor deprived a whole city of its freedom for having crucified Roman citizens
Clarke's manuscript addition, in which the magistrates confess they were ignorant the prisoners were righteous men and beg them to depart lest an insurrection be raised again
Ellicott's summary that the tables were turned and the accused had become a possible accuser
Calvin's inference that going straight to Lydia's house is a token that she was still the chief of the whole company in diligence
Clarke's closing note that great and lasting good was done by the visit, a church being founded whose members did credit to their profession
